p.t: In short
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: Risk reversal means the seller takes on the risk of a purchase, so the buyer feels safer and buys more.
A money-back guarantee works best when it is clear, strong, and has no hidden conditions.
A price-match guarantee is safe only for products whose suppliers force every seller to use the same price (MAP). Otherwise, do not offer it.
Before you set a return fee or a return window, check your supplier's return policy and your own profit left after costs.
Check your store's real limits for Shop Pay and other payment options before you show them to buyers.

Show a **small monthly payment** instead of the full price, and use this carefully.
Test a new payment option for **one month** against the old one before you keep it.
Measure how many buyers pick each price level, and test guarantee length against how many visitors buy.
Risk reversal: the principle and the decision rule
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: Risk reversal means **moving the risk** of a purchase from the customer to the seller.

Buyers are risk-averse, which means they dislike the chance of losing money.
If all the risk stays with the buyer, **conversion** (the share of visitors who buy) goes down.

Risk reversal can take the form of a **returns policy** (rules for sending items back).
It can also be a **price-match guarantee** (a promise to match a lower price elsewhere).

It can also be another satisfaction guarantee.
It can also be a worry-free installation or pre-assembled delivery for products that need setup.

A money-back guarantee is the **strongest** offer element.
The main reason buyers hesitate is **perceived risk**, meaning the feeling that something could go wrong.

A money-back guarantee makes any offer more attractive.
This only works if the **supplier** (the company that ships the product for you) is reliable and product quality is good.
Treat risk reversal as a **must-have** for making a lot of money in high-ticket dropshipping.
High-ticket means expensive products. Dropshipping means a supplier ships the product for you.

The customer must be protected if something goes wrong.
Place the guarantee **after the value stack**.

A value stack is the list of everything the buyer gets, with what each item is worth.
First build the value.
Then remove the risk with a money-back guarantee or another risk reversal.

Example of another risk reversal: a statement that it **costs nothing** if the buyer is not satisfied.
The guarantee then reinforces a strong offer.
Make the guarantee the **main headline** (the biggest line at the top of the page) when the guarantee is strong and the offer is clear.

A guarantee boosts response, meaning how many people reply or buy.
The better the guarantee, the **better the response**.

Strong guarantees outperform weak ones.
Some marketers claim guarantees are outdated.
Strong guarantees still outperform weak ones, even so.
If you make a big claim, the guarantee must have **no caveats** (hidden conditions or fine print).
A lowest-price guarantee should exclude only things like **secondhand products**.
Every extra rule or state-specific exception (a rule that applies only in some US states) makes the whole offer look **weak**.

A guarantee is more convincing when it comes from someone the buyer **knows and trusts**.
Example: a local dealer (a nearby shop or seller) who signs a written pledge to refund.
Risk reversal: the principle and the decision rule (continued)
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t:
A guarantee from a distant, unknown company is less persuasive.
Guarantees are not limited to products.
They can cover **service levels**, such as lowest fare, maximum downtime (how long a service may stop working), or a fixed meal service time.
Money-back and trial guarantees

Offer clear refund guarantees and money-back policies.
Set a **fixed time limit** for the guarantee.

If customers are unsatisfied, they get a **full refund**.
Guarantees remove purchase risk and build trust.
Guarantees directly raise **perceived value**, meaning how valuable the buyer thinks the product is.

Basic money-back guarantee: a **refund for any reason** if the buyer is not fully satisfied.
Use livelier words such as "delighted" or "thrilled".
If it is true, say why no competitor offers the same guarantee.

Refund and keep the premium: the buyer can cancel, get a **full refund**, and keep a free bonus gift (the premium).
This makes the guarantee feel generous and certain.

Redundancy means saying the same thing more than once. It also helps.
State the refund promise **two or three times** in different words.

Example: "a full refund of every penny paid".
A **30-day** money-back guarantee reverses the buyer's risk.

Loss aversion means people feel losses more strongly than gains. It makes this guarantee strong.
The shopper does not feel the purchase can go wrong.

Pattern: "[number] day money back guarantee, [condition or reassurance]".
A **clear time limit** turns a risky purchase into a reversible one.

Example: "60 day money back guarantee, no questions asked".
Example: "14 day money back guarantee on every order".
Pattern: a money-back guarantee tied to a **short, specific time and effort**, such as "results in X minutes a day or your money back".

It cuts the perceived time to results.
It reduces the effort required.
It lowers buying risk, which raises the value of the offer.

Use it **only after the product has been tested** and its quality is confirmed.
Example 1: "Ease your morning stiffness in 5 minutes a day or your money back."
Example 2: "See a cleaner kitchen in 2 weeks of 10 minutes a day, or get a full refund."
Trial periods and free examination
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t:
A trial period with a refund, such as **three to four days** or one week, lowers the buyer's risk.
It raises perceived value.

Offer it **only when** the business can afford the refunds.
Design the terms to keep the refund rate (the share of orders refunded) as low as possible.

Offer a free examination period (time to try the product before paying) of **6 days, one week, 10 days or 30 days**.
The free period comes before the buyer pays.

The seller pays shipping both ways, so returning the product costs nothing.
Make clear that the buyer owes **nothing** unless he keeps the product.

A free trial with a return window means the buyer can send the product back within a set time.
Example: a **full refund within 90 days**.

This turns the guarantee into a no-risk trial.
A **100-day** free trial or lifetime warranty can work for furniture-type brands.

Avoid a free-trial offer for a low-cost product that breaks often.
Avoid it for a stingy customer base (buyers who are unwilling to spend).
These cases cause problems.
Offer something the buyer can test before paying, such as **samples**, a week of use, or approval shipments (goods sent to be checked, then kept or returned).

Do not ask for a purchase up front.
Let the customer prove the product's claims at **no cost or risk**.

Case: a sewing motor was offered for a **one-week home trial**, with a technician who showed how to use it.
About **nine in ten** trials led to a sale.

The offer removed the risk of buying and let the product sell itself.
A "try, then pay" offer converts far better than a "try, then return if not satisfied" offer.

Once the customer has used the product, the decision to keep it is already made.
Where possible, **ship first and bill after use**.
Results-based and no-cost guarantees
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t:
Guarantee a result with a **no-saving-no-cost** offer.
Ship a full trial batch at your own expense.

Charge **only if** the buyer's measured saving meets the stated level, such as **25 percent**.
If the saving falls short, the buyer keeps the trial at no cost.

Just-pay-shipping offers: the product is free at checkout, and the customer pays shipping.
These offers can work.
But they look **scammy** (like a trick), so the brand needs careful positioning.
A variant requires a **minimum-spend subscription** after the free product. A subscription is a plan that charges again and again.

This produces **recurring revenue** (money that comes in again and again).
It also encourages use.

Offer a refund **only when** a buyer contacts you and says the content is not valuable.
Do not heavily advertise the guarantee.

Vague guarantees such as "satisfaction guaranteed" **fail**.
They set no expectation for the customer.

They seem risk-free but are not credible.
Specific guarantees work, such as "30-night money-back" or "7-day results or your money back".
Specific guarantees communicate confidence and clarity.
Example: the Posture Pro Corrector offered a **30-night** money-back guarantee at a **$39.99** price.
The ad claimed relief from back and neck pain in as little as **7 days**.
The guarantee removed purchase friction (anything that slows down a buy) by offering a full refund if the benefit timeline was not met.
The lower price ($39.99) compared with the discounted version ($49.99 regular, 20% off) suggests the offer is positioned as a **trial price**.
Timeframe logic: the 30-night refund period is set against a claimed benefit of "as little as 7 days".
The customer can check the benefit **well before** the refund deadline.
A **90-day** money-back guarantee with no questions asked was shown on the landing page (the single page a buyer reaches from an ad).
Guarantee wording and proof (continued)
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: It was also used in the ads as a risk reversal.
The guarantee is a USP (unique selling point, the main reason to buy from you). It sits next to the mechanism (how the product works) and the price.

Competitor pages can differ in guarantee length.
One page advertised a **90-day** 100% money-back guarantee.
Another advertised a **365-day** money-back guarantee.
Guarantee length is an offer element you can test against conversion rate (compare two versions and see which converts better).

A guarantee tied to a recognized seal or certification (an official mark of approval) should state a clear refund or replacement window.
Example: **two years**.

A concrete time limit reads as more credible than an open-ended promise.
Case: a seller mailed about **2,000 packages** with this guarantee.
The guarantee: pay $25, or donate $50 to charity, if the recipient read the whole letter, watched the video, listened to the audio, and still felt it was a waste of time.

The guarantee cost roughly **$100,000 at most**, if every claim was paid.
The mailing brought **10 to 15** appointments per 100 letters.

**2 to 3** of those appointments became clients.
Each client was worth about $10,000 in first-year value (money from them in year one).

Case: a seminar letter guaranteed the content.
The author paid out **less than $200** in claims.

The letter was mailed to nearly 4,000 prospects (people who might buy).
The author earned **over $100,000** in profit.
Split tests (sending two versions to different groups and comparing) showed that adding a letter guarantee increases readership and response.
Lower perceived risk on the landing page.
Show visible reassurance, such as a free trial period, easy cancellation, a money-back guarantee, and clear answers about returns, refunds, help, and what happens if the product is not wanted.

Place these **near the hero** (the large top section of the page) and the offer.
For subscriptions, use an **"easy cancel" message**.

The message states there is no contract and the customer keeps control.
Flexible subscription plans lower the fear of being trapped.
Returns and restocking fees (continued)
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: Returns and restocking fees
Return policy length should match each supplier's return policy.

A **30-day** return window (time to send items back) can be offered on products priced from $1,000 to $2,500. (2020)
Offer it **only when** the supplier accepts returns. (2020)

Cap the return window (set a limit on it) rather than offering unlimited returns.
Match the return policy to the supplier's policy.

Example: **30 days**, when the supplier allows 30 days.
Your return policy does not have to match a competitor's policy.
If the supplier does not accept returns for a product, set that product as **not eligible for returns**.
Set the restocking fee (a charge taken when an item is returned) **10 to 15 percent above** the supplier's restocking charge. (2023)

The extra covers return shipping costs. (2023)
Check competitors first. (2023)
Not charging a fee may affect conversions. (2023)
Return shipping fees can become the customer's responsibility if the return policy says so. (2023)
Check how top competitors word their return policies **first**. (2023)
Before matching competitors' restocking fees, which can reach **20 percent**, calculate your margin (the profit left after costs).

Also calculate before matching their upgraded delivery options.
Match those offers **only if** the margin still works after the cost.

Mistake: advertising a 30-day return or free returns while hiding a **25% restocking fee** destroys trust.
On a $1,000 product, that fee is **$250**.

Any return condition that makes the promise conditional must be stated plainly.
If you cannot state it plainly, do not make the promise.

Case: a seller changed the returns policy with little else changing.
Monthly revenue rose from about **$40,000 to $80,000**.

The source notes that this scale of increase is not typical.
Other businesses showed much smaller gains.
Return fee options: checkout plus
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: Checkout Plus is a paid option at checkout that makes returns free.

Average US return fees are around **$8 per return**.
The source estimated Australian fees at about $5 AUD.
The source said this needed double-checking, so treat that figure as **unverified** (not yet confirmed).

A common Checkout Plus baseline is a pre-purchase fee (paid before the buyer pays) of **$2.98**.
The later return fee in that baseline is **$10**.

These two figures are a starting point that suits many brands, not a fixed rule.
In the demo, the unlock fee was **$1.98** on a $600 snowboard.
The total was $601.98.

Without the unlock fee, a return triggered a **$12.00** handling fee (a charge for processing the return).
The store can exclude certain items from the service.
The right return fee depends on shipping rates, the product vertical (product category), product weight, and the brand's current return rate.
Heavy or bulky products, such as appliances or furniture, can carry higher fees.
Higher-AOV brands can carry higher fees too. AOV means average order value, the average amount spent per order.

Test fee levels before choosing one.
Example: **$2.99 against $3.99**.
Measure uptake (how many shoppers choose the option).

The vendor (the company that sells the software) recommends an A/B test (comparing two versions) first.
Do this **if a brand is skeptical** about adding a cart fee.

Checkout Plus is a pre-purchase option in the cart (basket) and checkout.
The shopper pays a small fee to get a **free return**.

This avoids a larger return fee later.
Shoppers who do not opt in (choose the option) pay the normal return fee if they return.

Checkout Plus can be framed as **peace of mind**, not insurance.
The shopper pays a small fee now.
This makes sure a later return does not cost **$10 to $15**.

Checkout Plus can be set up as a **flat fee** (the same every time) or a dynamic fee (it changes with the order).
It has many customisable options.
How it works (continued)
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t:
Package protection (insurance for the parcel) can be bundled with it.
The bundled fee is **higher** to cover both protection and free returns.

Package protection is priced by cart value (the total of items in the basket).
The source's understanding is that it is about **2%** of cart value.

The price rises when it is bundled with Checkout Plus.
Checkout Plus is **never added automatically** to the cart.
If the shopper does not opt in, it is not added at checkout.

This keeps the shopper's decision intact.
In the demo, the cart showed Checkout Plus at the bottom, with the price and a details pop-up (a modal).

Procedure:
1. The shopper **clicks the Checkout Plus button** in the cart.
2. At checkout, the option appears already selected or not, based on the cart choice, and the shopper **can change it**.
3. If the shopper later returns and opted in, the return is covered and **no handling fee** applies.
4. If the shopper did not opt in, the option still appears at checkout unselected, and a return triggers the **normal return fee**.
Example economics (the money math): with a **20% return rate** and 50% of shoppers opting in, the pre-purchase fees can **fully cover** return software

and return shipping costs.
Return software is the system that handles returns.
The vendor says it absorbs part of this cost too, meaning it pays part of it itself.
Pre-purchase revenue is roughly the share of shoppers who opt in, multiplied by (times) the fee.

Compare this with the share who actually return, multiplied by the return cost.
Vendor data cited about **70% opt-in** against typical return rates of 20-30%.

The gap between opt-ins and returns covers return operations (the work of handling returns).
That gap often leaves a **surplus** (money left over).

Shoppers who pay the fee are not necessarily the ones who return.
A cohort is a group of shoppers. The opted-in group's return rate was slightly higher.

The non-opted group's return rate was slightly lower.
So the **overall return rate** stayed stable.
Price match and price guarantees (continued)
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: Price match and price guarantees
Suppliers that enforce minimum advertised price (MAP, the lowest price a shop may advertise) forbid resellers from selling below a set price.

Because of this, a price guarantee is **low-risk**.
Competitors cannot legally undercut you (sell cheaper).
They rarely offer a lower price.

Most online shoppers do not know that dropship suppliers enforce MAP.
MAP requires all authorized retailers (approved sellers) to advertise at the **same price**.
Because customers do not know this, they compare prices across shops, looking for discounts that legally cannot exist.

This is why a price guarantee is a **powerful conversion tool**.
It appears to offer pricing assurance, which is genuinely true because of MAP.

It creates almost no refund liability (little risk of having to pay money back).
Price matching works with MAP products because all sellers keep the **same price**.

With non-MAP products, a competitor can cut prices by a large amount **at any time**.
You would be forced to match a price where no margin is left.

A non-MAP competitor can cut its price by as much as **30% within a week**.
A price-match promise can force you to sell with **no margin**.

Use price-match guarantees **only when** all sellers are bound by the same MAP.
The same MAP keeps prices equal everywhere.

A price-match promise only makes sense in MAP markets, where sellers keep one enforced price.
Matching costs little there.
Outside MAP, the same promise forces you to match prices on products you would sell at a **loss**.
Which suppliers can be covered
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t:
If your suppliers enforce MAP, **offer a price-match policy**.
Show it as a benefit on the site.

Competitors often do not have one.
Price-match guarantees **only apply to MAP suppliers**.
Do not offer one for suppliers without MAP.

Do not offer a price-match guarantee on **non-MAP supplier products**.
Price-match guarantees only make sense with MAP pricing enforced.
Products from non-MAP suppliers should be **excluded** from any price-match guarantee you offer.
Products from non-MAP suppliers should be excluded from the price-match guarantee.
A price-match guarantee on products without MAP can create conflicts with other sellers.

Exclude suppliers that do not enforce MAP from any price-match guarantee.
Otherwise, customers can force you to match a price that does not make money.

Do not offer a price-match policy on your website in markets without MAP.
Customers could ask you to match prices on products where you would **lose money**.

So the policy can only hurt you.
Suppliers without MAP can be excluded from the policy.
Those product pages should **not show** the policy.
A price-match guarantee is **optional**.
p.h: When to offer, and when to drop it

p.t:
Competitors offering a six-month price guarantee can influence buyers.
So a missing guarantee can **cost sales**.

A price-match policy can be left off, **especially at launch** (when the store first opens). (2023)
Customers who find a slightly lower price elsewhere may ask for a refund. (2023)

Remove the price-match policy when **most** of your suppliers do not enforce MAP. (2023)
A few brand exclusions are acceptable. (2023)

If **half or more** suppliers are non-MAP, do not list the policy at all. (2023)
Reason: it causes confusion. (2023)
Price-guarantee mechanics
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: The price guarantee applies to the price shown on the website **before any coupon code** (discount code) is applied.

If a competitor is cheaper, the store matches that price.
The guarantee should state this clearly.

If you promise a price match, state it in **one short line** on the page.
Link to the full policy.
The promise works as a trust element (a sign that builds trust) for resellers selling products that are also sold elsewhere.

A price-match policy, if offered, should be shown on the **product page**.
Buyers can see it without leaving.

A price-match guarantee page promises that the store aims for the best price.
It will match a lower price a customer finds at another online store.

It is one of the trust pages set up before launch (before the store opens).
The promise must be one the store can **actually keep**.
Write its conditions, such as the matching rules, **only after** the store has decided how it will handle them.
Contact your suppliers to ask about **extended warranty** options (longer protection after the normal warranty ends) and their pricing.
Extended warranties typically cost about **$25 per product** for one year of coverage.

If your customers value warranty protection, include the extended warranty **free** with purchases.
This helps you stand out from competitors.

Offer a warranty for expensive items as a **single checkbox** at checkout.
If the customer does not tick it, send an **automatic email** shortly after the purchase.
The email offers the warranty with a discount.
Extend.com is a Shopify app (an add-on for the online store software) for selling extended warranties on high-ticket products. (2023)
You earn a **commission** (a share of each sale). (2023)
Extend.com handles all warranty fulfillment (delivering the service), claims processing (handling warranty requests), and customer service. (2023)
Source A members recommend it as a way to add revenue **without additional operational complexity** (extra work to run). (2023)
Discounts and payment methods
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: Discounts and promo codes (discount codes) can be applied with **every payment method**.

This includes installment providers such as Klarna, a pay-later service.
Do not exclude installment payments from the discount.
Financing options: shop pay, klarna, affirm, PayPal credit

Shop Pay Installments is Shopify's option to pay in parts.
It is available for orders from **$35** up to **$30,000**.

Orders below $35 do not qualify.
The financing limit for a single purchase is **$30,000**.
Conflict: one source states that Shop Pay requires a minimum customer order value of **$40-50** to activate as a payment option.

The same source states that products under **$30** do not qualify.
The Shopify tier above lists $35.
Check the threshold in your own store's settings **before** setting any product price or messaging.
For orders from $35 to $50, customers can pay in **two** interest-free installments (no extra cost), every two weeks, of 50% of the total each.

Customers can also pay the full amount at checkout.
For orders from $50 to $999, customers can pay in **four** interest-free installments, every two weeks.

Example: an $800 order is paid over **about two months** with no extra cost.
For orders from **$150** up to $30,000, customers can pay in monthly installments.

Interest rates depend on each customer's credit approval with Shopify.
The merchant (the store owner) does not set or see these rates.

For orders above $25,000, the customer pays **$5,000 upfront** to Shopify.
The rest is split into equal monthly installments that carry interest (extra cost).

This case is rare and mainly applies to large B2B orders (sales between businesses).
Example: a hoodie priced at **$44.50** falls in the $35 to $50 tier.

The product page shows an option to pay two interest-free installments of $22.25 each.
Shoppers can ignore this and buy at full price, or choose the installment option at checkout.

The installment tiers and interest terms are preset by Shopify.
The merchant cannot change them.
The merchant decides **only whether** the option is switched on for the store.
Shop Pay financing limit
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t:
The Shop Pay financing limit varies by store. (2023)
It was originally **$500**. (2023)

It is now higher on many stores, but some stores still have lower limits. (2023)
Check the limit before assuming it covers your average order value. (2023)
If the limit is below your average order, **keep Klarna as a backup**. (2023)
Conflict: the **$30,000** per-purchase figure above applies to the Shopify installment programme as currently described.

The $500 original limit (2023) applies only where the store's own limit has not been raised.
Use the limit shown in your store settings as the governing value (the number that counts).
When deciding whether to offer Klarna alongside Shop Pay, first check whether your average order value fits within Shop

Pay's financing limit. (2024)
If Shop Pay's maximum financing covers your typical order size, **Klarna is not necessary**. (2024)
Add Klarna **only if** Shop Pay's limit is too low for your average order value **and** you want to offer more customers financing options. (2024)
Buy-now-pay-later services (BNPL, which let customers pay in parts over time, such as Afterpay and Klarna) increase customer acquisition (winning new buyers).

This is especially true across the **top five countries**.
The default risk (the risk that a buyer fails to pay) falls entirely on the customer's credit.
You receive **full payment upfront** from the BNPL provider.
This eliminates merchant chargeback exposure. A chargeback is when a bank takes money back from a seller after a buyer's dispute.

Offer payment options such as Shopify Pay installments, Klarna, or similar financing.
These let customers spread payments.

This matters **especially in weaker economic conditions**.
A financing app allows customers to pay in installments.

It directly increases conversion rate by removing upfront payment barriers.
This matters most for **price-sensitive buyers** (people who watch price closely).
Affirm and PayPal credit
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t:
Offer **PayPal Credit** (PayPal's pay-later credit) to customers.
It gives **six months with zero payments** and 0% interest.

Affirm (a pay-over-time service) integrates directly with Shopify.
Both options can be offered together.

Payment plan via PayPal Credit: a seller with a PayPal business account can offer this option on purchases **above $99**.
It offers six months with no interest and no payments.

The seller receives the **full amount right away**.
The buyer pays PayPal.
To accept PayPal Credit, use a **PayPal business account**.

Enable the option in the account settings.
If the option is missing, **contact PayPal through live chat** to set it up.

PayPal Credit is enough for a **typical order value**.
Stores with an average order value near **$10,000** use more customised financing options.
An **installment** is one part of a price, paid over time.

Concealed price means showing a small payment instead of the full price.
Show a **small monthly or installment payment** in place of the full price.
In one test, "$39.95", "2 payments of $19.95" and "3 payments of $19.95" produced **no difference** in sales.

Use payment framing carefully and **test it**, since it can lift the price a buyer accepts.
Case: a $5,000 business equipment item was sold as four payments of **$1,250**.
A premium version (the higher-priced, better version) at $7,000 was offered as eight payments of $875. That is a **lower monthly payment** than the cheaper version.

**72 percent** of buyers picked the higher-priced premium version.
For higher-priced items, split the payment into a **small first installment** and then monthly payments.
Examples: $5 down (paid first) with the balance over nine months, $1 a month for 12 months, or $2 a month for a large set.

A **low monthly amount** makes the decision feel small.
For illustration, a $1,000 product could be offered on a **12-month** payment plan.
Installment framing and payment plans (continued)
p.s: Risk reversal, guarantees and payment plans

p.t: The first payment would be roughly **$100**.
Showing that smaller first amount next to the full price can make a high price feel affordable to shoppers who would otherwise hesitate.
The **buyer** carries the payment duty (the obligation to pay), not the merchant (you, the seller).
Keep the installment terms **visible** at the price point and at checkout (the payment step), so the frame is not a surprise.
Procedure:
p.h: Testing and decision steps: Testing a payment option

p.t: 1. Run the Shop Pay vs. Klarna test for **one month**. Shop Pay is Shopify's fast checkout, which can split payments. Klarna is a separate pay-later service.
2. Review the last three months of sales and note the **Klarna transaction count** (the number of paid Klarna orders).

3. Remove Klarna from the site by **disabling** the payment method (the way buyers pay).
4. **Enable** Shop Pay installments.
5. Run for **exactly one month**.
6. After the month, compare: did Shop Pay transactions **exceed, match or fall below** the Klarna baseline (the starting number you compare against)?
7. **Decide** whether to keep both, switch, or revert (go back to the old setup).
Test **fee levels** (the price or charge options you could set) before choosing one.
p.h: Testing a fee or price level

p.t: Measure **uptake** (how many buyers choose each option) at each level.

Test **guarantee length** (how long the money-back promise lasts) against conversion rate (the share of visitors who buy).
Guarantee length is an offer element that can be measured.
